title: Klar
description: A statically typed, natively compiled language with Kotlin-style syntax and systems-level speed. No virtual machine or garbage collector, what you write is what runs.

sections.title: Overview & Philosophy
content: Klar is a statically typed, natively compiled programming language. It combines the readable, Kotlin-style syntax of a modern high-level language with the execution speed and predictable memory behavior of a systems language. Source code is compiled to LLVM IR and from there to native machine code, there is no bytecode and no interpreter.

sections.title: Design Goals
content: Klar is a statically typed compiled programming language designed to combine the readability of modern high-level languages with the performance of systems languages. This document describes Klar v{{version}}. The language is small on purpose: readability is preferred over feature count, and every feature has to justify its complexity.

-- Clarity: code reads the way it behaves -- Simplicity: few concepts, each with one clear job -- Predictable behavior: no hidden allocations, no hidden control flow -- Native performance: fast enough to compete with Rust and C++ -- Safe by default: low level control is explicit and only available through unsafe -- Small but expressive: structs and classes, traits, enums and expression based control flow cover most programs

content.title: Direct to native
content.subtitle: No VM, no GC
content: Klar compiles straight to LLVM IR and native machine code. Memory is released deterministically as soon as nothing references it anymore.

content.title: Predictable
content.subtitle: No hidden costs
content: No hidden allocations, no runtime tracing and no GC pauses. The compiler inserts reference counting code at predictable places.

content.title: Readable
content.subtitle: Kotlin-style syntax
content: Concise declarations, expression based control flow and type inference where the initial value makes the type obvious.

content.title: Safer memory
content.subtitle: No pointers
content: Pointer syntax and arithmetic do not exist. Low level control is opt-in through unsafe.

sections.title: Project Status
content: Klar is built together with its reference compiler Bloom, written in C#. Whatever is specified but not implemented yet is marked as planned.

rows: Working, better error recovery is planned
Working: diagnostics, completion, hover, go to definition, semantic colors

sections.title: Quickstart
content: A first program, then the rest of the language in order from simple to complex. The chapters after this one follow that order, starting with The Basics.

sections.title: Hello, Klar
content: Every program starts at a function called main.

content.title: main.kl

content: Line by line: -- from core.system import print makes the print function available in this file -- fun declares a function, functions are always written in camelCase -- main is the entry point -- no return type is written, so it returns Void, which means nothing

sections.title: Build and Run
content: The command line tool is called Bloom. It will compile a project to a native executable and run it.

content.code:
bloom build
bloom run

content: Bloom can parse and type check Klar code today, but turning it into an executable depends on code generation, which is not finished.

sections.title: Editor Support
content: A plugin for JetBrains IDEs adds syntax highlighting, semantic colors, code completion, hover information, go to definition and live error reporting for .kl files. It is backed by a language server built on the same lexer, parser and type checker as the compiler.

sections.title: The Basics
content: Everything a program needs before it does anything interesting: comments, variables, the built-in types and operators.

sections.title: Comments
content: Comments use the C style.

sections.title: Statements
content: A line break ends a statement. A semicolon ends it explicitly, which allows several statements on one line.

content.code:
val x = 1; val y = 2
val z = x + y

sections.title: Variables
content: A variable is introduced with one of three keywords. The type comes after the name and can be left out when the initial value makes it obvious.
-- val can be assigned once and is read-only afterwards -- var can be reassigned freely -- const is a compile time constant, inside a type it is also static

content.code:
val maxSpeed: Int = 200
var speed = 0
const MAX_PLAYERS = 4

speed = 50
// maxSpeed = 250   error: a val cannot be reassigned

content: Variables are camelCase. Constants are UPPER_CASE, so they stand out from everything else.

sections.title: Types
content: All built-in types are written in PascalCase.

rows: no value, the return type of functions that return nothing
a range of Int values, the end is not included

content: A number literal is an Int or a Float by default. A trailing L makes an integer a Long, a trailing d makes any number a Double and a trailing f makes any number a Float. In hexadecimal literals d and f are digits, so there only L works. An Int fits where a Long is expected and a Float where a Double is expected, but not inside arrays. Every other conversion between number types needs a cast such as Int::count.

sections.title: Strings and Characters
content: Strings use double quotes, characters single quotes. A string starting with $ is interpolated: anything inside braces is an expression. Three double quotes start a string that spans several lines.

content.code:
val name = "Klar"
val letter = 'K'
val greeting = $"Hello, {name}!"
val sum = $"1 + 2 = {1 + 2}"
val poem = """
Roses are red,
this string spans lines.
"""

rows: Mixing Int and Float gives a Float, a Long and an Int gives a Long, and a Double or a Long with a Float gives a Double. Dividing two whole numbers gives a Float, or a Double when a Long is involved
Equality needs both sides to have the same type. Structs compare their values, classes compare identity, see Equality
Work on Int, Long and Byte
A statement, it produces no value
Creates a Range, the end is not included

content.code:
val count = 10
val ratio = count / 4            // 2.5, a Float
val exact = Float::count / 4     // casts first, then divides
var total = 0
total += 5

content.title: Division
content: Dividing two Ints gives a Float: 10 / 3 is 3.333..., not 3. Assignment is a statement, so chained assignment like a = b = c does not exist.

sections.title: Functions
content: Functions package code under a name. Names are camelCase.

sections.title: Declaring Functions
content: A function has the keyword fun, a name, typed parameters and a return type after an arrow. Leaving the return type out means Void.

sections.title: Returning Values
content: The last expression of a function body is its result, so return is only needed to leave early.

sections.title: Expression Bodies
content: A body that is a single expression can be written after => instead of in braces.

content.code:
fun twice(x: Int) -> Int => x * 2
fun greet(name: String) -> String => $"Hello, {name}!"

sections.title: Control Flow
content: Control flow in Klar is expression based: if produces a value. This removes the need for a ternary operator.

sections.title: Conditionals
content: The condition is wrapped in parentheses. Each branch is a block in braces, or a single expression after =>. When the result is used as a value, every branch must have the same type and nullability, and an else is required.

content.code:
val label = if (count == 1) { "item" } else { "items" }

val sign = if (n > 0) => "positive"
    else if (n < 0) => "negative"
    else => "zero"

sections.title: While Loops
content: while repeats its body as long as the condition holds. break leaves the loop and continue skips to the next round. Both are only allowed inside a loop.

sections.title: For Loops
content: for walks over every element of an array or every value of a range. The end of a range is not included, so 1..4 covers 1, 2 and 3. The loop variable only exists inside the loop and its type can be written out if wanted.

sections.title: Arrays
content: An array type is the element type followed by []. Array literals use square brackets and elements are read with an index.

content.code:
val primes: Int[] = [2, 3, 5, 7]
val first = primes[0]
val grid: Int[][] = [[1, 2], [3, 4]]
val count = primes.length   // 4

content: length gives the number of elements as an Int. It is read only.

sections.title: Nullability
content: Types do not accept null by default. A question mark after the type makes it nullable. A non-nullable value can always be assigned to a nullable one, never the other way around.

sections.title: Custom Types
content: Types group data and behavior. Klar has structs and classes, plus enums for fixed sets of values. Their names are PascalCase.

Types have fields, functions and constructors. A constructor is written like a function without the fun keyword and carries the name of its type. A type can declare several constructors. A val field without an initial value has to be assigned in every constructor. Constructors are called by the name of the type, there is no new.

sections.title: Structs
content: A struct is a value type meant for small pieces of data, like a position, a color or a rectangle. Assigning it to a new variable copies it. A struct cannot inherit and cannot be extended. Inside a function of a struct, self is the instance.

sections.title: Classes
content: A class is a reference type for objects that have an identity, like a window, a texture or a database connection. Constructing it allocates the instance on the heap, and assigning it to another variable shares the instance. How its lifetime is managed is explained in Reference Counting.
A class can declare several constructors.

sections.title: Equality
content: The == operator means something different for the two kinds of type: -- Structs compare values: two structs are equal when all of their fields are equal -- Classes compare identity: two class values are equal only when they are the same instance, even if all their fields hold the same data

content.code:
val p = Point(1, 2)
val q = Point(1, 2)
val samePoint = p == q       // true, same values

val first = Player("Ace")
val second = Player("Ace")
val alias = first
val sameName = first == second   // false, two instances
val sameOne = first == alias     // true, one instance

sections.title: Enums
content: An enum is a fixed set of named values. Members are reached through the enum's name. An enum can give every member a value of one type.

sections.title: Abstraction
content: Sharing behavior between types.

sections.title: Traits
content: A trait is a promise: a list of functions a class has to provide. Trait names start with T. A class lists the traits it implements after a colon, and marks the implementing functions with implement.
A class can implement any number of traits, and a trait can build on other traits with the same colon syntax.

sections.title: Inheritance
content: A class can extend one base class and implement any number of traits. The base class is always listed first. Classes are closed by default: only a class marked open can be extended, and only a function marked open can be implemented again by a derived class. A derived class passes arguments to the constructor of its base class with base(...) after its own parameter list.

rows: the class can be extended, or the function can be implemented again
implements a trait function or replaces an open function of the base class

sections.title: Memory
content: Klar has no garbage collector and no pointers. Values live on the stack, class instances are reference counted.

sections.title: Stack and Heap
content: Local variables, structs and enums live on the stack and are released when their scope ends. Passing a struct to a function copies it, so the function cannot change the caller's value. A function that changes a struct hands the result back.

content.code:
fun moved(p: Point, dx: Int, dy: Int) -> Point {
    var result = p
    result.offset(dx, dy)
    return result
}

val start = Point(10, 20)
val next = moved(start, 5, 5)   // start is unchanged

content: Class instances live on the heap. Passing a class value passes the reference, so the function sees the same instance as the caller.

sections.title: Reference Counting
content: Every class instance carries a reference count. The compiler inserts the counting, you never write it.

-- Constructing a class allocates the instance on the heap and sets the count to 1 -- Copying a reference, by assigning it or passing it as an argument, increases the count -- When a variable goes out of scope, or a var is reassigned, the count of the old value decreases -- When the count reaches 0, the destructor runs and the memory is returned

sections.title: Weak References
content: Two instances that reference each other keep each other alive forever. Marking one side weak breaks the cycle: it does not count, and it reads as null once the target is gone. A weak reference therefore has to be nullable.

sections.title: Destructors
content: A destructor runs the moment the reference count reaches zero. It is the place to release things the language does not know about, like native handles. A destructor carries the name of its class and is introduced with destructor.

sections.title: Unsafe
content: An unsafe block marks code whose safety the compiler cannot check by itself. It does not introduce any new syntax: there are no pointers inside it either. Code in an unsafe block is written like all other code.
Unsafe is reserved for: -- calling native code through extern functions, which is only allowed inside an unsafe block -- manual memory operations implemented by the standard library

sections.title: Organizing Code
content: Modules, imports and visibility, for programs that outgrow a single file.

sections.title: Modules
content: A module groups declarations under a dotted lowercase name. It is either wrapped in braces or, when it is the only module of a file, declared once at the top and covers the rest of the file. Declarations outside of any module belong to the global module.

sections.title: Imports
content: Imports go at the top of a file. import makes everything of a module available, from picks single names. A module can be spread over many files.

content.code:
import game.core
from game.core import Player, Enemy

sections.title: Access
content: Every declaration can state who may use it. When the modifier is left out, the declaration is public.

rows: inside the same library or program
inside the type and the types extending it
inside the scope that declares it

sections.title: Modifiers
content: A declaration is written in a fixed order: annotations, access, modifiers, then the keyword.

rows: the class can be extended, the function can be implemented again, see inheritance
implements a trait function or an open function of a base class
a reference that does not count, see weak references
the function has no body, a native library provides it, see extern declarations

sections.title: Annotations
content: An annotation attaches information to the declaration that follows it. It is written with @. Arguments have to be constants. You can declare your own with annotation.

sections.title: Extern Declarations
content: extern marks a function that has no body here because a native library provides it. It is written among the modifiers. The @Library annotation names the library in its first argument. The optional second argument names the native function when it differs from the Klar name. Native functions have to be declared at module level and only use Int, Long, Float, Double, Bool, Byte, Char and String, which are mapped to their C counterparts. They can only be called inside an unsafe block.

content.code:
@Library("m", "sqrt") extern fun squareRoot(x: Double) -> Double

@Library("m") extern fun cos(x: Double) -> Double

content: A call goes through a generated wrapper with the Klar signature. Int, Long, Float, Double, Bool, Byte and Char map to int32_t, int64_t, float, double, int8_t, int8_t and uint16_t. A String is passed as a null terminated UTF-8 copy, and a returned const char* is copied into a new String. Other types cannot be passed to native code.
The first argument of @Library is linked: a plain name like m becomes -lm, a path or a file name with an extension is passed to the linker as it is.

sections.title: Casing
content: Casing tells you what a name is without looking at its declaration.

rows: fun struct class enum trait annotation destructor
if else while for in break continue return

sections.title: Operator Precedence
content: From loosest to tightest binding.
